a.headline: Beauty brands were writing slop before AI: here is how Uncommon won a D&AD Black Pencil for calling it out
a.summary: Uncommon Creative Studio turned a collection of hollow marketing buzzwords into a periodic table parody, winning the top D&AD prize for craft and wit. The project is a sharp lesson in how conceptual rigour and painstaking execution can outperform AI-generated filler content.

a.headline: We have the kind of stuff AI wishes it could make: Why trust is more important than ever for the NASA brand
a.summary: NASA brand leadership argues that authentic visual heritage and earned institutional trust cannot be replicated by generative AI tools. For students thinking about branding and authenticity, this piece asks what human-authored design assets are actually worth in an AI-saturated market.

a.headline: Born Social on the power of creators in the AI age
a.summary: Social-first agency Born Social argues that investing in human creativity is a competitive advantage as AI tools flood platforms with generic content. CCO Paddy Smith reflects on why authentic creator voices are increasingly the differentiator brands are paying for.

a.headline: The Daily Heller: Typographically Speaking, What Comes Next?
a.summary: The ITL Fonts and AI Conference is tackling how AI is reshaping type design and typographic practice at a moment of real industry anxiety. Type designer Nadine Chahine features in a conversation that every graphic design student thinking about the future of letterforms should follow.

b.headline: People are standing up and fighting back: the north Devon revolt against a vast AI datacentre
b.summary: Plans for one of Europe's largest AI campuses inside a UNESCO-designated biosphere reserve have triggered fierce local resistance in north Devon. The story puts a human and environmental face on the land and energy demands that underpin the generative AI tools designers use daily.

b.headline: The Data Center Backlash Should Also Be a Climate Reckoning. It Isn't Yet
b.summary: Climate advocates are trying to attach environmental accountability to the growing public opposition against data centres, but the carbon and water costs of AI infrastructure remain underreported. This piece is a useful primer on why the tools powering generative design carry a hidden ecological price tag.

b.headline: Democracy blindsides Silicon Valley power players looking to transform the world with AI
b.summary: Communities across the US and Europe are pushing back against the siting of AI data centres, raising questions about who bears the local costs of global AI infrastructure. The piece connects the democratic deficit in AI expansion directly to the energy and land pressures that the industry rarely acknowledges.

b.headline: AI is dominating the conversation at Climate Week
b.summary: At New York Climate Week, AI's energy consumption emerged as a central flashpoint alongside the usual debates about fossil fuels and net zero targets. For design students, this is a reminder that every prompt submitted to a generative tool connects to a broader and contested energy economy.

c.headline: Joseph Clark on why he is keeping AI out of Oh Studio, and the protest film that went viral saying so
c.summary: Animation director Joseph Clark made a film called We Are Better Than This that went viral this summer, arguing that AI has nothing meaningful to offer his practice or his studio. This is a direct and personal account of building a creative business as an act of resistance against AI adoption in motion design.

c.headline: Matthew Maldonado on why LAIKA made everything by hand for new film Wildwood
c.summary: The stop-motion studio behind Coraline and Kubo and the Two Strings continues to build every puppet and set physically by hand, making a quiet but powerful case for analogue craft in an industry being reshaped by digital and AI production. Art director Matthew Maldonado explains why the slowness and difficulty of physical making is precisely the point.

c.headline: British celebrities beat AI companies lobbying to get free use of their work. They have a warning for Australia
c.summary: A coalition of UK artists and creatives successfully pushed back against attempts by AI companies to train on their work without consent or compensation, and they are now urging other countries to follow. This is a critical story for design students to understand in terms of copyright, labour and the political fight over who owns creative output.

c.headline: Who Moved My Work? Tim Thompson on RevThink's The Weekly Briefing
c.summary: Industry consultant Tim Thompson challenges motion designers to think critically about the long-term structural shifts AI and client self-sufficiency are causing in the value of creative work. Rather than panic, he argues for a clear-eyed reassessment of what skilled practitioners actually offer that automation cannot replace.
